query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Wear-induced mechanical removal of the protective oxide layer on the eutectic HEA repeatedly exposes fresh metal surfaces, thereby accelerating localized corrosion and overall degradation at elevated temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA with a finely lamellar microstructure that has formed a nominally protective oxide/passive film on both the fcc and B2 phases.
generation.intervention: Application of sliding wear in a corrosive environment at elevated temperature that mechanically disrupts the oxide film.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (700°C–800°C) exposure in a chloride-containing acidic medium under reciprocating wear conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity of the protective oxide film on the different phases, whose removal exposes reactive fresh surfaces.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear continuously removes or damages the protective oxide layer, preventing stable passivation. This repetitive exposure leads to accelerated localized corrosion since freshly exposed metal reacts rapidly with the environment. The differential oxide formation on fcc and B2 phases further contributes to heterogeneous corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a static corrosion test without mechanical wear, samples undergoing wear will suffer significantly increased degradation, with deeper pits and higher material loss due to the cyclic removal and reformation of the oxide layer.
generation.baseline: The alloy exposed solely to elevated temperature corrosion without mechanical wear, allowing a relatively intact oxide film to form and offer protection.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies when the oxide film, although protective under static conditions, is vulnerable to mechanical chipping under dynamic wear, particularly in corrosive media at high temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: While the general principle of wear-induced oxide removal is well established, precise quantitative rates of oxide reformation versus removal, and their differential impact on the fcc and B2 phases, remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical HEA samples and subject them to high-temperature corrosion tests with and without imposed sliding wear. Use in situ high-temperature SEM with a corrosion cell and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to monitor oxide layer integrity and measure local pit depths and wear track profiles over time.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to track oxide film stability
High-temperature SEM imaging of oxide removal events
Profilometry for wear track depth and pit depth analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples undergoing wear do not exhibit a significantly higher rate of oxide removal and subsequent increases in corrosion damage relative to non-worn samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: ABSTRACTThe ongoing demand for high‐thrust turbine engines necessitates the advance of next‐generation structural materials capable of withstanding higher temperatures. Commercial MCrAlY alloy, used as bond coats crucial for thermal barrier coating (TBC) systems, face a fundamental temperature ceiling of ∼1100 °C due to accelerated oxidation and spallation. Here, we design a novel Y and Hf co‐doped NiCoCrAl‐type multi‐principal element alloy (MPEA) that achieves exceptional 1200 °C oxidation resistance primarily through lattice distortion‐induced diffusion suppression. Compared with typical NiCoCrAlY alloy, the MPEA exhibits 59% lower in thermally grown oxide (TGO) growth rate, as well as negligible TGO spallation after 500 h at 1200°C. This performance stems from a significantly refined eutectic structure enabling rapid formation of a protective Al2O3 scale during initial oxidation, coupled with lattice distortion that elevates vacancy formation energy and Al migration barriers within the Al‐depletion zone (ADZ), drastically reducing sustained diffusion rates. This co‐design strategy, integrating tailored microstructure and lattice distortion, establishes a new paradigm for ultra‐

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Based on the above conclusions, the corrosion process of the EHEA in the test solution is schematically described in Figure 14. The passive films of few Al-Ni-rich phases are attacked by Cl− at lower temperature (Figure 14a2), and then occurs localized corrosion (Figure 14a3); while the passive films of Al-Ni-rich phases are damaged (Figure 14b2), and more Al-Ni-rich phases are dissolved at higher temperature (Figure 14b3). Metastable pits are preferentially created on the grain boundary or B2 phase. Pitting is enhanced by the effect of polarization. Due to autocatalysis by the caustic ions, the metastable pits gradually grow in the pitting corrosion area or the selective dissolution region. Moreover, the size of the selective dissolution region increases with temperature, and pitting occurs on the surface at various temperatures.
